label: eq:replica-poisson-product-identity
title: Proof
body_md:
First recall the Poisson product identity, including its short proof.
For disjoint sets \(B_r\) of finite intensity \(\nu(B_r)\), their counts \(N_r\) are independent Poisson variables.
Thus a function equal to \(f_r\) on \(B_r\) and to one elsewhere satisfies
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{E}\prod_j f(X_j)
  &=\prod_r\mathbb{E} f_r^{N_r}
  =\prod_r\sum_{k=0}^\infty
    e^{-\nu(B_r)}\frac{\nu(B_r)^k f_r^k}{k!}
  =\exp\ab\{\int(f-1)\,\mathrm d\nu\ab\}.
  \label{eq:replica-poisson-product-identity}
\end{align}
Approximation by simple functions gives this identity for \(f=e^{-h}\), \(h\geq0\), by monotone convergence, and for other integrands whenever both sides and the approximation are integrable.
Independent marks are included by replacing \(\nu\) with intensity times mark distribution.
The same simple-function calculation gives \(\mathbb{E}\sum_j h(X_j)=\int h\,\mathrm d\nu\) for \(h\geq0\).

For any independent scalar or vector mark \(c\), substitution \(r=s\lVert c\rVert^2\) gives
\begin{align}
  d_\alpha\int_0^\infty
    \mathbb{E}[1\wedge s\lVert c\rVert^2]s^{-1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm ds
  &=d_\alpha\mathbb{E}\lVert c\rVert^\alpha
    \ab[\int_0^1r^{-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm dr
       +\int_1^\infty r^{-1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm dr]
  \\
  &=\frac{4d_\alpha}{\alpha(2-\alpha)}
    \mathbb{E}\lVert c\rVert^\alpha.
  \label{eq:replica-marked-summability}
\end{align}
If this quantity is finite, there are almost surely only finitely many terms with \(s_j\lVert c_j\rVert^2>1\), and the sum of the remaining terms has finite expectation.
Consequently, \(\sum_j s_j\lVert c_j\rVert^2<\infty\) almost surely.
Taking \(c_j=\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v_j\), the partial Gaussian sums, conditional on \(\{s_j,\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v_j\}\), form an \(L^2\)-bounded martingale and converge almost surely and in conditional \(L^2\).
Their characteristic function is
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{E}\exp\ab(i\sum_j\sqrt{s_j}g_j\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v_j)
  &=\mathbb{E}\exp\ab(-\frac12\sum_j s_j(\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v_j)^2)
  \\
  &=\exp\ab\{d_\alpha\int_0^\infty
    \mathbb{E}_{\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v}\ab[e^{-s(\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v)^2/2}-1]
    s^{-1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm ds\ab\}.
  \label{eq:replica-conditional-gaussian-series}
\end{align}
Here the second equality is \eqref{eq:replica-poisson-product-identity}.
Using \(\mathbb{E}_g e^{i\sqrt{s}gz}=e^{-sz^2/2}\) and then \eqref{eq:replica-levy-khintchine} proves \eqref{eq:replica-stable-poisson-transform}.

label: eq:universality-small-frequency-expansion
title: Proof
body_md:
Let the generative function of $X$ as $\phi_X(t)=\mathbb{E} e^{itX}$.
  Symmetry and the normalized tail in
  Equation~\eqref{eq:stable-domain-universality-tail} give
  \begin{align}
    \log\phi_X(t)
    &=
    -\left|t\right|^\alpha+\left|t\right|^\alpha\eta(t) ,
    \label{eq:universality-small-frequency-expansion}
  \end{align}
  where $\eta(t)\longrightarrow0$ as $t\to0$.

  For the replicated empirical measures considered in the saddle calculation,
  assume for each fixed $n$ and $\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k\in\mathbb{R}^n$ that
  \begin{align}
    D^{-1/\alpha}
    \max_{1\leq i\leq D}\left|\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol u_i\right|
    &\longrightarrow0\\
    \sup_D\frac1D\sum_{i=1}^D
    \left|\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol u_i\right|^\alpha
    &<\infty.
    \label{eq:universality-infinitesimal-replica-array}
  \end{align}
  Independence across feature coordinates and
  Equation~\eqref{eq:universality-small-frequency-expansion} then give
  \begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}\exp\ab(
      iD^{-1/\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^D
      X_i\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol u_i)
    &=
    \exp\ab(
      -\frac1D\sum_{i=1}^D
      \left|\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol u_i\right|^\alpha
      +o_D(1)
    )
    \\
    &=
    \exp\ab(
      -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\rho_D\ab(\mathrm d\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v)
      \left|\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol v\right|^\alpha
      +o_D(1)
    ).
    \label{eq:universality-asymptotic-stable-feature-average}
  \end{align}
  Indeed, the absolute remainder in the exponent is bounded by
  \begin{align}
    &\max_{1\leq i\leq D}
    \left|\eta\ab(D^{-1/\alpha}\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol u_i)\right|
    \frac1D\sum_{i=1}^D
    \left|\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol k^\top\@ifstar\mathbf\boldsymbol u_i\right|^\alpha.
    \notag
  \end{align}
  which vanishes by Equation~\eqref{eq:universality-infinitesimal-replica-array}.
  Equation~\eqref{eq:universality-asymptotic-stable-feature-average} is
  Equation~\eqref{eq:replica-stable-feature-average} up to $o_D(1)$.
  Assuming this error is uniform under the Fourier integral in
  Equation~\eqref{eq:replica-single-factor-fourier}, the one-sample factor
  satisfies
  \begin{align}
    \mathcal I_{n,D}^{P_X}[\rho_D]
    &=
    \mathcal I_n^{S\alpha S(1)}[\rho_D]+o_D(1).
    \label{eq:universality-one-sample-factor-replacement}
  \end{align}
  The other terms in the replica action do not depend on the feature distribution.
  Since $N/D\to\kappa$, Equation~\eqref{eq:universality-one-sample-factor-replacement}
  therefore gives
  \begin{align}
    \mathcal S_n^{P_X}[\rho,\hat\rho]
    &=
    \mathcal S_n^{S\alpha S(1)}[\rho,\hat\rho]+o_D(1).
    \label{eq:universality-replica-action-replacement}
  \end{align}

  From Equation~\eqref{eq:universality-replica-action-replacement} onward,
  the saddle variation, replica-symmetric ansatz, replica limit, and
  zero-temperature limit are exactly those in
  Appendix~\ref{app:replica-derivation}.  The RS solution therefore
  gives Equation~\eqref{eq:stable-coefficient-error-universality}.
